name: RU-59063

lead: RU-59063 is an early nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor very tightly. It is sometimes classed as a SARM, and muscle circles occasionally link it to lean mass, though that link is theoretical.

It was first described in 1994, derived from the antiandrogen nilutamide, and bound the rat androgen receptor with up to about three times the affinity of testosterone, with mixed antagonist and weak agonist behaviour. Its main significance is as a starting point for later drugs such as enzalutamide and apalutamide, and for radioligand research. No muscle or appearance studies in people exist.

paras: It is a laboratory compound that was never marketed, so there is no routine for use.
Human safety is unstudied, and it has no approved use.

angle.text: RU-59063 is a 1990s research androgen-receptor ligand, sometimes classed as a SARM, which muscle circles occasionally link to lean mass. It binds the androgen receptor tightly and became a template for later antiandrogens. It has no human use, and its appearance link is theoretical.

lead: RU-59063 is an experimental nonsteroidal androgen, sometimes classed as a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM), first described in 1994. It was never marketed and has no clinical use [1][2]. It appears in appearance and muscle discussions because SARMs as a class are researched for building lean mass and bone, and androgen-receptor compounds are of interest to people seeking more muscle or other androgen-driven changes.

It was derived from the antiandrogen nilutamide and bound the rat androgen receptor with very high affinity, reported as up to about three times that of testosterone, with little binding to other steroid receptors [3]. It was first thought to be a potent antiandrogen; later work found dose-dependent androgenic activity, with lower efficacy than dihydrotestosterone [1].

Its main role in the literature is as a prototype and laboratory tool: it served as a starting point for second-generation antiandrogens such as enzalutamide and apalutamide, for radioligand research, and as a tritiated marker for androgen receptors [1][3][4][5]. No human studies exist.
infobox: Ki about 2.2 nM; about 3-fold testosterone (rat AR), 8-fold (human AR) [1][3]

paras: RU-59063 is an N-substituted arylthiohydantoin with the molecular formula C17H18F3N3O2S, derived from the first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogen nilutamide [1]. In the 2000 and 2004 radioligand work its structure is described as 4-[4,4-dimethyl-3-(4-hydroxybutyl)-5-oxo-2-thioxo-1-imidazolidinyl]-2-trifluoromethylbenzonitrile, and iodine was substituted for the trifluoromethyl group in analogues [4][5].

Wikipedia reports an androgen receptor Ki of about 2.2 nM, with roughly 1,000-fold selectivity over progesterone, estrogen, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors, and affinity up to 100-fold higher than flutamide, nilutamide or bicalutamide for the rat receptor; the compound was initially assumed to be purely antagonistic but was later found to include partial androgenic effects [1]. The 1994 study described the arylthiohydantoin series as having exceptionally high receptor affinity and no binding to other steroid receptors, and reported that, unlike testosterone, RU-59063 showed no specific binding to human plasma; the lead compound was tritiated for use as a research marker [3]. A 1997 cell study classed RU-59063 as a partial agonist/antagonist at the androgen receptor [2].

Chemists later made iodinated analogues of RU-59063 to develop radioiodinated androgen receptor ligands for imaging. One analogue, DTIB, showed subnanomolar binding affinity (Ki 0.71 nM) for the rat androgen receptor and agonist activity comparable to dihydrotestosterone in a cell-based assay [4]. A 2004 structure-activity study of iodinated arylhydantoins and arylthiohydantoins reported that side chains such as hydroxybutyl or methyl gave the highest affinities (Ki 0.71 to 11 nM), while bulky lipophilic side chains were poorly tolerated [5]. Basic-science studies also used it to examine how androgen receptors interact with DNA response elements [2]. The second-generation antiandrogens enzalutamide, RD-162 and apalutamide were derived from RU-59063 [1].

Wikipedia's article on selective androgen receptor modulators says the first nonsteroidal SARMs were developed in 1998 and that the term was introduced in 1999 [6]. It reports that several trials of SARMs raised lean mass but that it is unclear whether strength and function also improve, and that as of 2023 no SARM had been approved by the FDA or European Medicines Agency [6]. The World Anti-Doping Agency banned SARMs in 2008, and SARMs sold online as research chemicals have been reported to be frequently mislabeled [6]. These statements concern the class and not RU-59063 specifically, which is not an approved or marketed product.
No studies found. All published work is laboratory or animal research on receptor binding and chemistry.
